content.title: Postgres Partial Indexes in Practice
content.text:
A partial index covers only the rows that match a WHERE clause. When your hot query always filters on the same predicate and that predicate selects a small slice of a big table, a partial index is smaller than a full one, faster to scan, and cheaper to maintain on writes. This walkthrough builds one, proves it works with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and covers the cases where the planner will refuse to use it.

The example table is a job queue:

CREATE TABLE jobs (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  status text NOT NULL,
  queue text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  payload jsonb
);

In production it holds about 40 million rows, of which almost everything is done or failed. Only a few thousand are pending at any moment. The worker polls with this query:

SELECT id, payload FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'pending' AND queue = 'email'
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 100;

Before adding anything, capture a baseline. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) in front of the query. On a table with no useful index you will see something like this:

Limit (actual time=2140.512..2140.538 rows=100 loops=1)
  -> Sort (actual time=2140.510..2140.521 rows=100 loops=1)
       Sort Key: created_at
       -> Seq Scan on jobs (actual time=0.031..2098.774 rows=3412 loops=1)
            Filter: ((status = 'pending') AND (queue = 'email'))
            Rows Removed by Filter: 39996588
Planning Time: 0.212 ms
Execution Time: 2140.601 ms

Two seconds, a full sequential scan, and forty million rows thrown away to find three thousand. A regular index on (status, queue, created_at) would help, but it would index all 40 million rows to serve a query that only ever looks at the pending ones.

Create the partial index instead. Use CONCURRENTLY on a live table so it does not block writes; note that this cannot run inside a transaction block:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY jobs_pending_email_idx
ON jobs (created_at)
WHERE status = 'pending' AND queue = 'email';

The index key is created_at because that is the sort order the query wants. The status and queue columns do not need to be in the key at all: every row in the index already satisfies the predicate, so the ORDER BY can be served by walking the index in order and stopping after 100 rows.

Run the same EXPLAIN ANALYZE again:

Limit (actual time=0.041..0.198 rows=100 loops=1)
  -> Index Scan using jobs_pending_email_idx on jobs (actual time=0.039..0.184 rows=100 loops=1)
Planning Time: 0.298 ms
Execution Time: 0.231 ms

The sort is gone, the scan reads 100 rows and stops, and execution drops from 2140 ms to well under a millisecond. Check the size difference too: SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('jobs_pending_email_idx')) will report a few hundred kilobytes, where a full index over the same columns on 40 million rows would be well over a gigabyte.

Now the part that bites people. The planner uses a partial index only when it can prove the query's WHERE clause implies the index predicate. That proof is simple and literal. These variations will all fall back to a sequential scan or a different index:

First, a parameter instead of a literal. If your driver sends WHERE status = $1 AND queue = $2 as a prepared statement with generic plans, the planner cannot know that $1 is 'pending' at plan time, so it cannot use the index. Either inline the constants for this query or ensure the driver uses custom plans; in PostgreSQL 12 and later, SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan is a blunt but effective fix for the session.

Second, a wider predicate. WHERE status IN ('pending', 'retrying') is not implied by status = 'pending', so the index is ignored. Build the index with the same IN list if that is the real query.

Third, a missing conjunct. WHERE status = 'pending' with no queue filter is also not implied, because the index does not contain pending jobs for other queues. You would need a separate index with just the status predicate.

When in doubt, copy the predicate from the query into the CREATE INDEX statement verbatim, and run EXPLAIN on the exact query shape your application sends rather than a hand-typed version in psql. If you see Seq Scan where you expected the partial index, compare the Filter line in the plan against the index predicate character by character. The mismatch is almost always there.

Finally, rows leave the index when their status changes away from pending, so on a very high-churn queue consider lowering autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor on this table to keep the index compact.

notes: Solid how-to with concrete before/after plans and a real list of planner pitfalls (prepared statement parameters, predicate implication). A correct judge should rate it useful and accurate, above generic content but not groundbreaking.
